title: Where is the post office?
goal: Ask for and give directions, and set up the second case: the locative — the only case that never appears without a preposition in front of it.
bekal: ask for directions and understand the answer
put nouns into the locative after *v*, *na*, *o*, *pri*
choose between *v* and *na* — a choice you can't guess from the meaning

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Neviem, kde som
dialogs.intro: Budi is lost near Hlavná stanica, the main station. He stops a woman walking past.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, may I ask you something?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kde je pošta? Neviem, kde som.
lines.id: Where is the post office? I don't know where I am.
lines.literal: where is post? not-I-know, where I-am.

lines.speaker: Pani:
lines.text: Pošta je na námestí, oproti kostolu.
lines.id: The post office is on the square, opposite the church.
lines.literal: post is on square-loc, opposite church-dat.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: And how do I get there?

lines.speaker: Pani:
lines.id: Go straight on and then turn left.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rovno a doľava. Je to ďaleko?
lines.id: Straight and then left. Is it far?
lines.literal: straight and to-left. is it far?

lines.speaker: Pani:
lines.text: Nie, päť minút pešo. Je to hneď za parkom.
lines.id: No, five minutes on foot. It's just behind the park.
lines.literal: no, five minutes-gen on-foot. is it right-away behind park-ins.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: A je tam blízko aj banka?
lines.id: And is there a bank near there too?
lines.literal: and is there near also bank?

lines.speaker: Pani:
lines.text: Áno, banka je vedľa pošty, v tej istej budove.
lines.id: Yes, the bank is next to the post office, in the same building.
lines.literal: yes, bank is next-to post-gen, in that-loc same-loc building-loc.

notes: **Na námestí, v budove, za parkom** — three prepositions, three different endings. The first two are locative, the third instrumental (unit 17). For now just notice that **a preposition always changes the word after it**; not a single Slovak preposition leaves its noun untouched.
**Môžem sa niečo opýtať?** is the most polite way to stop a stranger. Gentler than asking straight away, and it almost always makes people stop gladly. Put *prepáčte* in front of it.
**Choďte** is the polite command form of *ísť* (to go). The casual form is *choď*. You don't need to produce it at A1, but you must recognize it — every set of directions you hear will use this form.
**Nie je za čo** literally "there is nothing for what" — the standard reply to thanks, a little warmer than *prosím*. Both are correct.

**Aj means "also", like *tiež*.** The difference is position: *aj* stands right before the word it highlights (*aj banka* = a bank **too**), while *tiež* usually comes at the end or after the subject (*Ja tiež* = me too). At A1 you can use them interchangeably in simple sentences.

grammars.title: The locative — the case that can't stand alone
body: The locative is the only one of the six cases that is **never** used without a preposition. That's good news: you don't have to guess when to use it — if *v*, *na*, *o*, *pri*, or *po* comes in front, the ending is locative.

head: Noun type
Ending
Nominative
Locative
rows: **m / n ending in k, g, h, ch**

after: **The adjective changes too**: m and n take **-om** (*vo veľkom dome*, *v malom meste*), f takes **-ej** (*vo veľkej škole*). Two endings, twenty seconds to learn.

**The second row often surprises people.** Words ending in *k, g, h, ch* take *-u*, not *-e*, because an *-e* ending would force that letter to soften and change its sound. That's why it's *na Slovensku* and not *na Slovensce*. It's also why *v parku*, *v Rakúsku*, *v Nemecku*.
**Notice *v* becomes *vo*** before words starting with *v* or *f*: *vo Viedni* (in Vienna), *vo februári*. Just like *z/zo* and *s/so* — purely so the mouth doesn't trip.

grammars.title: V or na — a choice you can't guess from the meaning
body: Both mean "in/at", both take the locative, and no rule covers a hundred percent. But there's a tendency that covers about ninety percent, and that's more than enough for A1.

head: v — enclosed spaces, towns, countries
na — surfaces, institutions, events
rows: *v dome* — at home, in the house

after: **Look at the seventh and eighth rows.** Almost every country takes *v*, but Slovakia itself takes **na Slovensku**. So do *na Ukrajine* and *na Morave*. The reason is historical — these regions were once part of a larger kingdom, and *na* has stuck ever since. For beginners: learn *na Slovensku* as one chunk, because you'll say it every day.

**A pattern you can hold on to:** *v* for something you **go inside**, *na* for something you **go to** or whose surface you're on. The post office takes *na* because Slovak sees it as an errand you go to, not a building you enter.
**If you pick the wrong one, you're still understood** — it's a mistake that makes Slovaks smile, not frown. But picking right sounds very polished, so learn the table above a few rows at a sitting.

blocks.text: The last column isn't decoration — it's part of the word you must learn. If you note down *pošta* without *na pošte*, you've only learned half the word. This habit is what stops the cases from feeling like a table.

English

to the left / on the left

blocks.text: Look at the pairs **doprava/vpravo** and **doľava/vľavo**. The *do-* form means movement ("to the right"), the *v-* form means position ("on the right"). Slovak separates motion and rest everywhere — the same split comes back with *do/v* in unit 11.

English
rows: Can you show me on the map?

blocks.title: One sentence that saves the day
items: *Prepáčte, hľadám poštu.* — "Excuse me, I'm looking for the post office." Swap the last word for any place in the accusative, and you have one sentence that works all over Slovakia.
If the answer is too fast: *Pomaly, prosím* or *Môžete to zopakovať?* (Could you repeat that?). Both are polite and always work.
Excuse me, may I ask you something?
Go straight on and then turn left.
The bank is next to the post office.
